terms.definition: A sheet exactly two lipid molecules thick that separates one space from another, behaves as a liquid within its own plane, and controls what crosses it. The everyday sense of a thin separating sheet, as in a drum skin or the film inside an eggshell, keeps only the separating part. The plasma membrane is the one enclosing the whole cell.

Two facing layers of lipid molecules with their water-avoiding tails buried between them and their water-attracting heads exposed to water on each side. It is the structural core of every biological membrane and is about 5 nanometres thick overall, with a water-avoiding interior of about 3 to 3.5 nanometres.

Having both a water-attracting and a water-avoiding part in the same molecule. A phospholipid is amphipathic: a phosphate-containing head that water accommodates, and two hydrocarbon tails that it does not.

The tendency of water-avoiding molecules in water to cluster together. Water must reorganise into ordered cage-like arrangements around such a molecule, which costs free energy, and the cost falls when the water-avoiding parts group so that fewer water molecules are affected. It is what assembles a bilayer and what holds one together, because no bond joins one lipid to its neighbour.

One of the two layers of lipid making up a bilayer. In a plasma membrane the outer or exoplasmic leaflet faces the space outside the cell and the inner or cytoplasmic leaflet faces the cytoplasm. The two hold different lipids, and this lesson treats that difference as one of the two main organising facts about membranes.

Movement of a lipid or protein within the plane of one leaflet, past its neighbours. It is fast: a lipid swaps places with a neighbour about ten million times a second, giving a diffusion coefficient near one square micrometre per second, so a lipid crosses a cell-sized distance in a couple of minutes.

Movement of a lipid from one leaflet of a bilayer to the other, which requires dragging its water-attracting head through the water-avoiding interior. Spontaneous flip-flop is rare, less than once a month per molecule in synthetic bilayers, and an established difference between the leaflets takes days to run down without enzymes.

A qualitative summary of how easily the hydrocarbon chains in a bilayer move and how loosely they pack. The measurable quantities behind the word are viscosity and chain order; this lesson uses it as a direction of travel rather than as a number, which is what the outcome asks a learner to predict.

The change of a bilayer between a liquid state, with chains bending and lipids sliding past one another, and a rigid crystalline state with the chains packed straight and parallel. The temperature at which it happens falls when chains are shorter or carry cis double bonds, and cholesterol obstructs the transition.

A small, rigid, largely water-avoiding molecule with one hydroxyl group, wedged among the hydrocarbon chains of animal membranes, where it can be up to 40 per cent of plasma-membrane lipid. It restricts chain movement in a fluid bilayer and also obstructs crystallisation, so it buffers a membrane against change rather than pushing fluidity in one direction, and it lowers permeability to small water-soluble molecules.

The homeostatic adjustment of membrane lipid composition that holds membrane viscosity roughly fixed as growth temperature changes, chiefly by varying the proportion of packing-disrupting chains such as unsaturated or branched ones and by varying chain length. The ability is broadly conserved across living things.

The maintained difference in composition between the two leaflets of a membrane. In a eukaryotic plasma membrane, phosphatidylcholine and the sphingolipids sit mainly outside while phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine and the phosphoinositides are held inside. Slow flip-flop lets the difference persist; ATP-driven transporters create it.

A P4-ATPase that spends ATP to move specific phospholipids, phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine among them, from the outer leaflet to the cytoplasmic one. Flippases are what establish and maintain lipid asymmetry. A floppase is the corresponding ATP-driven transporter working in the reverse direction, and belongs to the ABC transporter family.

A transporter that moves phospholipids in both directions across a bilayer without specificity and without ATP, randomising the distribution between the leaflets. Switching one on abolishes an asymmetry the cell has been paying to maintain, which is how exposed phosphatidylserine becomes a signal.

A protein embedded in the bilayer itself, typically crossing it, and not removable by gentle extraction that leaves the bilayer intact. Integral proteins diffuse laterally and rotate about an axis across the membrane, and they do not flip-flop, so the side each part of the protein faces is fixed for its working life.

A protein attached to one face of a membrane through interactions with other proteins rather than embedded in the bilayer, and releasable by gentle treatments such as extreme pH or high or low salt that leave the bilayer intact.

The face of an epithelial cell that looks onto the lumen. In an intestinal absorptive cell it forms the brush border, carries an unusual lipid composition, and does the barrier and nutrient-uptake work.

The face of an epithelial cell that looks onto its neighbours and onto the basement membrane beneath the sheet. It carries a different set of lipids and proteins from the apical face of the same cell, and its business is contact with the tissue rather than with the lumen.

The apical specialisation of an absorptive intestinal cell: thousands of finger-like microvilli, each about a micrometre long and about a hundred nanometres across, raising apical surface area roughly thirtyfold. Its membrane is unusually rich in glycolipids, which with cholesterol and sphingomyelin form ordered domains that give it stability against the lumen.

A patch of membrane in which glycolipids, sphingomyelin and cholesterol pack more tightly and move less freely than the surrounding bilayer, while still remaining fluid. Such domains form in the outer leaflet and are unusually large and stable in the enterocyte brush border. The model of these domains remains under active discussion in the field.

The account of membrane structure set out in 1971 to 1972, in which proteins sit within and upon a fluid lipid bilayer and components diffuse within the plane. Mosaic never implied that components are evenly spread; uneven distribution within membranes was already being observed in the 1960s.

The sterol fungi build into their membranes where animal cells use cholesterol. It does the same structural job and is a different molecule, and that difference is what amphotericin B binds and what makes the drug more toxic to a fungus than to us.
